1.pericope_label: The murrain on the cattle, and Israel severed

schools.summary: Gill calls the sparing of Israel's herds a marvellous separation, since they shared the same air, water and pasture, and passes on the Targum's guess that Pharaoh sent as far as Pelusium to check. Calvin reads the divine title as a taunt teaching Pharaoh that the God he thought repelled was still in the field, treats the naming of the plague as God's hand as setting it against natural and accidental causes, argues that this apparently lighter stroke was heavier in its consequences since dead herds impoverish for years, calls the statement that all the cattle died a synecdoche, and sees in the enquiry a man compelled to learn what he would rather not have known.

Henry makes the unchanged demand the whole trial, whose word shall stand, hears the reasonableness of God's claim in the words my people and his jealousy in his willingness to give Egypt for their ransom, notes that the stroke falls without Aaron's rod, and that those who had made Israel poor were now made poor themselves. He observes that what men make an idol of God justly removes, recalling that Israel learned the calf in Egypt, and allows Pharaoh's enquiry no motive better than curiosity or reprisal.

Clarke distinguishes the two divine names as eternal power and as Supporter, resolves the difficulty by reading all the cattle that died as Egyptian, and infers that Egypt must have seen the vanity of its animal worship when its sacred beasts perished among the common herd. Wesley joins Henry in acknowledging God's hand in the sickness and death of beasts, since a sparrow does not fall without the Father.

Ellicott observes that Israel had shared the first three plagues, which brought annoyance without loss, and that the exemption begins here and probably continued unmentioned; he explains that because murrain is common in the Delta God marked this one by a fixed day, by sparing Israel and by striking every beast left in the field, and notes that the day's delay let a believing Egyptian house his cattle. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the plague-word as that which sweeps away, make the appointed hour the mark distinguishing judgment from season, and take all in its popular sense, restricted to the cattle in the field.

debates: How all the cattle died can be reconciled with the survivors assumed later. Calvin calls it a synecdoche for a general destruction; Keil and Delitzsch take all in a popular sense and confine it to beasts in the field; Clarke reads it as meaning that all which died were Egyptian.
How far Israel had been exempt before. Ellicott holds they shared the first three plagues, which cost them nothing, and dates their exemption from the fourth.
outliers: Clarke's remark that after seeing their deified animals die among the common herd, one might have supposed Egyptian animal worship could never maintain its ground again.

8.pericope_label: The boils, the rout of the magicians, and the hardening

schools.summary: Gill pictures the ashes falling like hot sleet across the kingdom, and observes that the magicians, though they had attempted no imitation since the lice, had stayed about Pharaoh belittling the miracles and were justly punished. Calvin notes that God now executes without threatening, since admonition had become useless, and refuses to soften the hardening into mere foreknowledge while insisting the tyrant's hardness was still voluntary; he also observes that boils on cattle prove not every beast had died before.

Henry sees the plague rising from the cattle to men's own bodies because lesser judgments had failed, and reads the furnace ashes as God showing men their sin in their punishment, the furnaces of Israel's oppression becoming the terror of the oppressors. He itemises the justice of the magicians' punishment, for hardening the king and for making sport of earlier plagues, so that those who would produce lice produced boils instead, and calls wilful hardness punished by judicial hardness the sorest judgment on this side hell.

Clarke draws the same congruity from the brick-kilns, describes the boils as among the most poignant afflictions short of death and asks what a multitude of them must occasion when one throws the body into a fever, locates them in the glandular parts, reports an old chronicler's account of blisters bursting and breeding worms, and notes that the magicians could neither imitate nor cure the plague and are never mentioned again. Wesley describes it as a burning scab that quickly raised blisters, and joins in reading judicial hardness as the punishment of wilful hardness.

Keil and Delitzsch derive the two Hebrew words from roots meaning to be hot and to swell, and identify the natural substratum with the Nile-blisters that appear as the inundation closes, which the Egyptians call the heat of the Nile. Ellicott identifies the furnace as a brick-kiln and makes the Egyptians' own wrongdoing the whip that scourged them, reads the sprinkling as a presenting of the ashes to God in evidence of Israel's wrongs, concedes such complaints are common in Egypt but rarely severe or shared with beasts, lists four marks of the miracle, suspects the magicians had come expressly to withstand Moses, and dates the judicial hardening from this point.

debates: Whether the magicians were present by chance. Ellicott suspects they came to withstand Moses, since the plague struck them hardest; Gill has them lingering to belittle the miracles.
outliers: Clarke's report from an old chronicler that the blisters burst with tormenting pain and bred worms.
Calvin's observation that boils breaking out on cattle prove not every beast had died in the previous plague.
themes: the furnace turned against the furnace-masters
enchantments that could not save the enchanters

13.pericope_label: The seventh summons, and the word that Pharaoh was raised up

schools.summary: Gill takes the threatened plagues for all that God had determined rather than the hail alone, reads the pestilence sentence as a past condition contrary to fact since no such destruction ever occurred, understands the raising up as preservation from earlier plagues and reservation for greater ones while allowing it may include God's eternal appointment, and hears in the final reproach a trampling that makes a highway of God's people. Calvin holds that threats are renewed not in hope of a cure but to expose obstinacy, says the strokes must now reach the bowels since battering the sides had failed, prefers the sense of preservation on the ground that a victory over a tyrant felled at once would have been less illustrious, and insists that behind the long-suffering lies eternal prescience, Pharaoh having been predestinated before his birth as the instrument of wrath.

Henry finds the difficulty in a demand made of a heart God has just hardened, and reads the demand as both a punishment fitted to a king who required bricks without straw and a pattern of long-suffering. He says God can plague the heart by making it senseless or hopeless, which are the worst plagues, and draws the moral that God sometimes raises bad men high and spares them long that he may be the more glorified in their fall.

Clarke argues that the Hebrew verbs about the pestilence are past and that the English future creates a contradiction, since neither Pharaoh nor his people were so destroyed; on the raising up he renders caused thee to subsist, claims the agreement of critics of almost all creeds, and denies that the Hebrew, Paul or the Greek can support the doctrine that God appointed and hardened this man from eternity in order to display power in destroying him — so man speaks, he says, but thus God has not spoken. He also notes that Pharaoh might still have submitted at this point. Wesley grants the whole description of Pharaoh as marked for ruin and providentially matched with Moses, but distinguishes the event from the design, scripture often speaking so of outcomes rather than intentions.

Ellicott describes the coming blows as meant to beat the heart down until it should yield and let the whole people go, concedes that the pestilence clause admits a future rendering but rules that the context forbids it, and glosses the raising up as being kept alive not for desert nor even in pity but only to show God's power. Keil and Delitzsch gloss the reproach as a military figure, the king damming himself up like a rampart against God's people.

debates: How a threat of pestilence and being cut off can stand when neither occurred. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott independently take the verbs as a condition contrary to fact — what God might have done and did not — with Clarke holding that the English future creates the contradiction.

What it means that God raised Pharaoh up. Ellicott and Clarke confine it to being kept alive; Calvin allows that sense but grounds it in eternal predestination; Clarke denies that reading outright as words God has not spoken; Wesley separates the event from the design; Gill permits both.

Why God delayed the final stroke. Calvin says a tyrant felled in one trifling engagement would have made a less illustrious victory; Clarke says the delay gave further opportunity to manifest that Jehovah alone is God.
outliers: Calvin's remark that nobody would believe a man could resist God with such headstrong folly unless this picture had been set before us.
Clarke's appeal to critics of almost all creeds, and his flat verdict that the predestinarian reading is how man speaks and not how God has spoken.
Wesley's rule that scripture often speaks of an outcome in language that sounds like intention.
themes: obedience required of a hardened heart
a threat that was never executed
raised up, or merely kept standing

18.pericope_label: The hail foretold, and the warning to house the cattle

schools.summary: Gill reads the warning as evidence of both the certainty and the terror of the plague and of God's remembering mercy in the midst of wrath, and Calvin lists five marks proving the hail unnatural — the named day, the named hour, its unexampled violence, its reach across the whole land, and the exemption of Goshen — and calls it a portent transcending nature rather than moisture frozen in mid air; he alone hears no mercy in the warning, reading it as an insult to the king's confidence and a challenge issued in the certainty of victory

Clarke says the hour was named to teach Pharaoh that the elements Egypt worshipped were God's creatures and now its executioners, defends the phrase to rain hail as physically exact since rain freezes as it falls and the stone grows by what it gathers, adduces modern storms at Liverpool and in Italy by way of parallel, and ends with the treasures of the hail in Job and the reflection that God with such artillery may desolate a world; on the warning he says simply that in the midst of judgment God remembered mercy and every life might have been saved. Wesley glosses the comparison as dating Egypt from its founding as a kingdom.

Ellicott measures the plague against the local climate, where rain and hail occur but thunderstorms are rare and mild, one fatal storm having been thought remarkable enough to cause universal consternation, and shows how easily the warning could have been obeyed, since the yearly inundation obliged Egypt to keep abundant shelter for cattle beside its mounded villages. Keil and Delitzsch treat the advice as a sign of divine mercy that would still have rescued the hardened man, and as proof that submission remained possible and the hardening was not yet complete.

debates: Whether the warning was mercy or mockery. Gill, Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch all read it as clemency, the last making it proof that Pharaoh could still have submitted; Calvin denies any sparing intent and takes it for an insult to the king's confidence.

How far the storm was natural. Clarke explains the physics of hail formation and lines up comparable modern tempests; Calvin marshals five marks to prove it could not have arisen from natural causes; Ellicott simply notes how rare damaging hail is in Lower Egypt.
outliers: Clarke's catalogue of later hailstorms, including one said to have killed the beasts, the birds and even the fish.
Calvin's observation that an ordinary tempest flies like an arrow within narrow limits, whereas this one covered the length and breadth of the land.
Ellicott's point that the inundation had already obliged Egypt to build shelter enough for every beast in the country.

22.pericope_label: The hail falls, with fire, and Goshen is spared

schools.summary: Gill passes on the rabbinic verdict that fire mingled with hail was a miracle within a miracle, since neither quenched nor melted the other, and notices that Egyptians dwelling among the Israelites escaped with them, drawing the rule that wicked men often fare better for the people of God among them. Calvin asks why the rod was needed when the hail had already been predicted, concludes that the command followed the prediction and so tried Moses' faith, holds that the gesture served to renew his commission for the contests ahead, and takes the whole as proof that the senseless elements stand ready to obey their Maker.

Henry makes the clouds both the storehouses from which God drops fatness on his people and the magazines from which he draws artillery against his enemies, notes that the corn already risen was destroyed while what had not yet come up was spared, and that God directs the clouds to rain or hail on one city and not another.

Clarke renders the word for thunder as voices, meaning repeated peals, insists that the fire literally walked upon the earth as a devouring and irresistible flame rather than a flash, notes that the electric fluid is essential to hail in any case and was here supplied in supernatural abundance, and calls the sparing of Goshen a signal proof of particular providence.

Ellicott gives the same literal rendering of the fire and reports the division between those who take it for ordinary lightning and those who see something more, inclining to the latter on the ground that electrical discharges sometimes persist as fire-balls, and appealing to the description of a fire infolding itself; he restrains every tree to the breaking of boughs and twigs, and compares familiar hail damage to crops. Keil and Delitzsch likewise deny that every herb and every tree are absolute, set out what was climatically normal — storms between December and April, at the season when cattle are at pasture — and locate the supernatural in the prediction, the exemption of Goshen and a fury that impressed Pharaoh more than all the previous plagues.

debates: Whether the fire was ordinary lightning. Clarke and Ellicott both read the Hebrew as fire walking on the earth, Ellicott reporting commentators on both sides and favouring a persistent electrical phenomenon; Gill treats the combination as a miracle within a miracle.

How far the words every herb and every tree extend. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both refuse an absolute sense, the one by comparison with the earlier all the cattle, the other by limiting the damage to boughs and twigs.

Why the rod was used when the plague had already been announced. Calvin infers that the command came after the prediction, making the gesture a renewal of Moses' commission rather than a sign for Pharaoh.
outliers: Gill's rule, drawn from the Egyptians living in Goshen, that wicked men often fare the better for the people of God among them.
Keil and Delitzsch's observation that the storm fell in exactly the months when Egyptian cattle are turned out to pasture.

27.pericope_label: Pharaoh confesses, and Moses goes out of the city to pray

schools.summary: Gill sets out the possible senses of the plea for it is enough, reports the rabbinic reason that Moses left the city because it was full of idols but prefers privacy, and suggests he also wished to show he did not fear the storm. Calvin grants that the words amount to true repentance and draws from them that sinners honour God's justice only by condemning themselves, but denies the reality, holding that terror makes even honest promises which the wicked break as soon as the fear lifts, as Saul did with David; he reads the departure from the city as a judgment on an unholy place, argues that God's dominion appears most clearly when he heals the wounds he inflicted, admires the nerve of a prophet who condemned the whole court to its face, distinguishes alarm from the true fear that is the beginning of wisdom, and explains the intercession as an interval granted so that the king's impiety might betray itself again.

Clarke brings out the emphasis of the Hebrew, that the Lord alone is the Righteous One and Pharaoh and his people alone the Sinners, and marvels that such a confession could be followed by fresh hardening; he hears in the plea a plain surrender, glosses the mighty thunderings as voices of God after the Hebrew idiom for a superlative, and marvels that so full a confession could be followed by fresh hardening.

Ellicott attributes Pharaoh's greater alarm to a plague that took human life and had not yet ceased, notes that the king who once called the Israelites idlers now blames only himself and his people, and faults the confession only for dividing a guilt that was almost wholly his own; on the promised knowledge he explains that Egyptians believed each country had its own gods and that Pharaoh had got no further than treating Jehovah as the God of the Hebrews, whereas the point was to have him owned as God of the whole earth.

debates: Whether the confession was sincere. Clarke and Ellicott take the words at face value and are astonished by what follows; Calvin holds that terror produced them without repentance, while denying that Pharaoh lied on purpose.

What the words for it is enough mean. Gill offers three constructions; Calvin rejects the reading that has Pharaoh congratulating himself on a lull and prefers a man beaten down by the continuing storm.
Why Moses prayed outside the city. Gill reports the rabbinic answer about idols but prefers privacy and courage under the storm; Calvin makes it a statement that the king's dwelling was unholy.

Why Moses interceded for a man he did not believe. Calvin answers that the reprieve was granted to let the impiety show itself and so fulfil what God had said of the remaining plagues, and denies that ministers may rest in a verbal confession.
outliers: Calvin's judgment that only a miraculous restraint kept the court from killing Moses where he stood.
Ellicott's note that the confession's one flaw is sharing out blame that belonged almost wholly to the king.
themes: the Righteous One and the sinners
prayer carried out of an unholy place
the God of the whole earth

31.pericope_label: The ruined crops, the storm stilled, and the relapse

schools.summary: Gill reports the opinion that the surviving grain was rice rather than rye, since rye is scarcely known there and grows too fast, has Moses retire into the field for undisturbed prayer, and notes that the heart grew harder as soon as the plague lifted. Calvin reads the sparing of the later crops as a remnant of hope left to invite repentance if the wickedness were curable, and makes the relapse a rule of the reprobate mind, which takes a short truce for a settled peace and presumes on impunity, observing that Moses aggravates the crime by recording that he had foretold this obstinacy himself.

Clarke supplies a traveller's account of Egypt's double seed-time and harvest, canvasses the versions for the disputed second grain and admits the Hebrew cannot be settled, and guesses the rod was in the outspread hands. He closes by arguing that the hardening verbs often mean no more than permission, that Pharaoh's heart is said to harden only after each miracle was seen and each plague removed, that he lay under no fatal necessity, and that men who sin with the Bible in their hands make Pharaoh look almost a saint. Wesley repeats that Moses went out both for privacy and to show he dared face the storm, and that his prayer opened and shut heaven as Elijah's did without subduing a hard heart.

Ellicott uses the state of the flax and barley to fix the date of this plague and help date the others, rejects rye as a grain never grown in Egypt and identifies the Hebrew word with the sorghum called doora, explains the escape of the later crops by the month's difference in ripening, and observes that a king never so deeply moved before must have made a greater effort of will to harden himself, so sinning the more. Keil and Delitzsch treat the note as an accounting of what was lost and what remained to lose, and confirm it from the reaping seasons given by the old authorities.

debates: What the second grain was. Gill favours rice, Clarke reviews spelt and summer wheat before admitting the Hebrew cannot be settled, and Ellicott rules out rye as never grown in Egypt and identifies the word with sorghum.

Why the later crops were spared. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch explain it by the calendar, the ear being still undeveloped; Calvin makes it a deliberate remnant of hope held out to invite repentance.

What the hardening means. Clarke argues the verbs often signify permission and that the hardening always followed the sight of a miracle and the lifting of a plague, so that Pharaoh lay under no necessity; Calvin treats the relapse as what security always does to a reprobate mind.
outliers: Clarke's closing turn on the reader, that a man sinning with the Bible in his hand makes Pharaoh, hardened against ten plagues, look a saint beside one hardened against ten millions of mercies.
Ellicott's quotation of a modern description of Moses standing bareheaded under the storm, safe because the hairs of his head were numbered.
Clarke's note that one old translator, unable to construe the verse about the grains, omitted it altogether.
themes: a plague dated by its crops
